Cartography has never been a neutral craft. Every map is an argument about what matters, made by deciding what to leave out. A road atlas erases rivers that a hydrological survey would treat as its whole subject, and a political map draws borders with a confidence that the ground beneath them rarely shares. The projection itself carries a claim: Mercator preserves angles at the cost of area, so it flatters the high latitudes and shrinks the equator, and generations of schoolchildren absorbed a picture of the world in which Greenland rivalled Africa. None of this is deceit exactly. A map that recorded everything would be the size of the territory and just as hard to read.

The domestication of yeast is one of the stranger collaborations in the human record, because for most of its length neither party knew the other was there. Bread and beer predate microbiology by thousands of years, and the practices that sustained them were transmitted as craft rather than as theory: keep back a portion of yesterday's dough, wash the vessel but not too well, work in the same room your mother worked in. What was actually being preserved was a population of organisms, selected generation after generation for tolerance of alcohol, of acidity, of the particular temperature of a particular kitchen.

Standardisation tends to be told as a story of engineers agreeing, but it is more often a story of engineers being compelled. Railway gauges did not converge because the arguments for a common width were finally understood; they converged because breaking bulk at every border became more expensive than rebuilding track. Screw threads, shipping containers, mains voltage, character encodings: in each case a plurality of locally sensible choices persisted until the cost of translation exceeded the cost of capitulation, and then one option won, not always the best one.

A coastline has no definite length, which sounds like a riddle and is actually a measurement result. Walk it with a metre rule and you will record a longer distance than you would with a kilometre chain, because the shorter instrument follows inlets the longer one steps across, and the pattern does not stop as you shrink the ruler. Every bay contains smaller bays. The number you report is therefore a property of your procedure as much as of the shore, and the honest way to state it is as a relationship between scale and length rather than as a single figure.

Musical tuning is a compromise nobody is entirely happy with. The intervals that sound most consonant correspond to simple frequency ratios, but those ratios do not close: stack twelve perfect fifths and you arrive very slightly above where seven octaves should have put you, a discrepancy known as the Pythagorean comma. Something has to give. Various temperaments distribute the error differently, sweetening some keys at the expense of others, and equal temperament spreads it uniformly so that every key is equally and slightly wrong.

The archive is a technology of forgetting as much as of remembrance. To keep everything is to keep nothing findable, so archivists appraise, and appraisal means destruction on a scale that would alarm most people who imagine the archive as an attic. What survives is shaped by what seemed administratively significant at the moment of transfer, which is why the correspondence of ministries outlives the correspondence of households, and why the daily texture of ordinary life is reconstructed from accident: a shopping list used as packing, a diary kept for a bet.
